metadata.title: Adult Literacy Skills and Risk of Job Automation Among Middle-Aged and Older Workers in the United States
metadata.venue: New Horizons in Adult Education and Human Resource Development

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the PIAAC 2012/2014/2017 U.S. Restricted Use File (RUF) and restricts the analytic sample to respondents aged 50+ who are employed. The authors explicitly state that survey weights are used to compute weighted descriptive statistics and to run survey-weighted linear regression predicting job automation risk. They also note that sampling and replicate weights are applied for the descriptive table, but the specific weight variable names are not reported in the excerpt. Because the analysis is a survey-weighted regression (not an ML algorithm), the paper’s weighting approach is appropriate for complex survey inference; however, the manuscript does not provide the exact replicate-weight method or variable names needed for full reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to PIAAC U.S. Restricted Use File respondents who are (1) age 50 years and older and (2) employed. The authors further exclude respondents with missing values for adult literacy skills scores and any covariates, resulting in an analytic sample of n=1,880; they report that the excluded proportion for missingness is <1% given available job automation risk information.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (Model 2): Adult literacy skills b = −0.052 (SE = 0.016), p = .002; R-squared = .189; job automation risk mean = 37.75% (SE = 0.622).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012/2014/2017 (U.S. RUF) data for employed adults age 50+ years, the study leveraged adult literacy skills alongside income quintile, educational attainment, living with a spouse, and gender to predict job automation risk (0%–100%), finding that higher adult literacy skills were associated with lower job automation risk (b = −0.052, p = .002) with the final model explaining about 19% of the variance (R-squared = .189). This indicates that strengthening adult literacy through adult education and training may reduce older workers’ exposure to automation-related employment insecurity, though the cross-sectional regression cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes a nationally representative PIAAC U.S. Restricted Use File sample of employed adults aged 50+ (n=1,880) using PIAAC adult literacy skills (0–500, estimated with 10 plausible values) to predict job automation risk for occupations (0%–100%). Job automation risk is constructed by mapping 43 PIAAC occupation sub-major groups to 31 sub-major groups and then to broader occupational categories using Frey and Osborne’s approach adapted by Yamashita and Cummins. The authors run survey-weighted linear regression and report that adult literacy skills are negatively associated with job automation risk in the final model (b = −0.052, SE = 0.016, p = .002), with R-squared = .189; the mean job automation risk is 37.75%. Limitations include reliance on an occupation-level automation-risk classification and the inability of regression on observational data to infer causal effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper does not evaluate machine-learning algorithms; it uses survey-weighted linear regression to model a continuous outcome (job automation risk). Therefore, ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and ml_techniques.primary is left null because no ML model comparison or ML learner is reported. The extraction still captures the empirical predictive relationship between adult literacy skills and automation risk using the study’s regression results.
